title: Counting outs & estimating equity
description: Six questions covering out counting, dirty outs, and the Rule of 2 & 4.

questions.prompt: You hold 9♠ 8♠ on K♠ 7♥ 6♣. How many clean outs do you have to make at least a straight on the turn?
questions.explanation: Open-ended straight draw: any 5 (4 cards) or any 10 (4 cards) makes a straight. 4 + 4 = 8 outs. The flush is irrelevant here because only one spade is in your hand.

questions.prompt: You hold A♠ 5♠ on K♠ 4♠ 3♥. How many outs do you have to a flush or wheel straight without double counting?
questions.explanation: Flush draw is 9 outs (the remaining spades). A 2 of any suit makes the wheel — but the 2♠ is already in your flush outs. The clean extra outs are the 2♥, 2♦, 2♣. 9 + 3 = 12.

questions.prompt: You're on the flop with 9 outs and getting all-in for the rest of the hand. Which figure best approximates your equity to win at showdown?
questions.explanation: Two cards to come and you're paying once → Rule of 4: 4 × 9 ≈ 36%. The exact value is ≈35.0%, very close.

questions.prompt: When does the Rule of 4 over-estimate enough that you should switch to (3n + 8)?

choices.text: Always — Rule of 4 is never accurate.
When n > 8 outs, two cards to come.
When you have a single overcard.

questions.explanation: For n > 8 the Rule of 4 over-counts cards that could appear on both turn and river. Phil Gordon's (3n + 8) refinement is much closer to the exact value above 8 outs.

questions.prompt: If villain bets the flop and you suspect they will bet again on the turn, you should still apply the Rule of 4 to your current draw to compute your call equity.
questions.explanation: The Rule of 4 only applies when you pay a single price to see both cards (e.g. all-in on the flop). With more betting to come, apply the Rule of 2 per street so that the future decision is priced in.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are reasons to discount or remove an out?

choices.text: The card completes your flush but pairs the board, plausibly giving villain a full house.
The card is the same colour as your hole cards.
The card completes your gutshot but also puts a four-flush on the board against a strong bettor.
The card improves your hand to top pair, top kicker.

questions.explanation: Dirty outs improve your hand but also improve villain to a likely better hand. Pairing boards and four-flush rivers are the canonical examples. Hand colour is irrelevant; TPTK is an *improvement*, not a dirty out.
